matter_reference_date_basis: matter_reference_date in candidates/matters/M047.json, taken from the exam session OCTOBER 2022. The law is applied as it stood at that date, and the enrichment dates the proposed Deed of Gift to 14 October 2022 so that the temporal test has a fixed point.
corpus_gaps: No rate instrument for stamp duty. Western Province Financial Statute s.37 and Stamp Duty Act s.2 both charge duty at the prescribed rate, and Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3 leaves the rate to a Ministerial Order in the Gazette. No Order, regulation or rate schedule is in the corpus, so the quantum question M047-Q02 cannot be answered.

The corpus holds only one provincial finance statute, the Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990. The enrichment therefore places the property in the Western Province; a matter concerning land in any other province could not be answered from this corpus.

The Western Province Financial Statute text in the corpus is visibly OCR-damaged: s.37 has transposed words, the definition labels in s.106 are lost so that the definitions of Transfer and gift run on from the preceding entry, and the definition of value in paragraph (c) prints the first limb marker as absent and the second as (ii). The parallel and cleaner text of Stamp Duty Act s.71 is recorded alongside it as a check.

No amendment to the Western Province Financial Statute is in the corpus and the section records carry no amendment events, so it is not possible to confirm from these sources alone that ss.37, 48, 51 and 106 stood unamended in October 2022.

A Deed of Gift of a house and land at Maharagama is an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, so it is chargeable with stamp duty at the prescribed rate. questions.authority_requirement_reason: What value must be stated in a deed of gift for stamp duty is answered by the charging section, the rule that duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, and the statutory definition of value for gifted immovable property acquired after 31 March 1977. Each of those is in the corpus, and none of them needs a judicial gloss or a rule of Roman-Dutch common law to be applied to these facts.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a Deed of Gift of a house and land in the Western Province is an instrument chargeable with stamp duty, a gift being gratuitous.
On what amount stamp duty on that deed is calculated: the price paid in 1977, that price plus the cost of improvements, or the present market value.
Which paragraph of the statutory definition of value applies where the donor acquired the property in December 1977, and how the two limbs of that paragraph are compared.
What figure the attesting notary must therefore set out in the deed.

questions.hop_count_basis: Four necessary linked steps: (1) the charging section catches an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property in the Province; (2) the interpretation section defines Transfer to include a gift, bringing the deed into charge; (3) s.48(1) directs that duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed; (4) the interpretation section defines value for gifted immovable property acquired after 31 March 1977 as the lower of two computed limbs. The notary's duty under s.78(2) hangs off the figure so computed rather than adding a further step. Verifier: raised from four to five. On the researcher's own convention a definitional bridge counts as a hop, and the step from the charge to s.48(1) needs the definition of 'conveyance' in s.106 (PROV-M047-901), because s.48(1) is keyed to property 'conveyed' and not to a 'transfer'.

enrichment.original_background: Rohan Perera purchased a house and property in December 1977 for Rs.250,000/-, and done improvements to the house to the value of Rs.800,000/-. The property is presently valued at Rs.6,500,000/-. He wishes to gift the said property to his son Wasantha.
enrichment.enriched_background:
Rohan Perera purchased a house and property in December 1977 for Rs.250,000/-, and done improvements to the house to the value of Rs.800,000/-. The property is presently valued at Rs.6,500,000/-. He wishes to gift the said property to his son Wasantha.

The property is Lot 12 depicted in Plan No. 2456 dated 3 March 1974 made by K. B. Wijesinghe, Licensed Surveyor, in extent fifteen decimal five perches, together with the two storeyed dwelling house bearing Assessment No. 47/3, Pathiragoda Road, Maharagama, within the Divisional Secretary's Division of Maharagama in the District of Colombo, Western Province. Rohan Perera bought it outright and at arm's length from an unrelated seller by Deed of Transfer No. 1187 dated 12 December 1977 attested by S. A. Dissanayake, Notary Public, and the Rs.250,000/- he paid was the open market price of the land and house on that date. The improvements costing Rs.800,000/- were an additional upper floor, a garage and a boundary wall, all built between 1996 and 1999, that is after he bought the property and before the deed he now proposes. He is the sole owner, the property is free of any mortgage or lease, and he intends an outright gift, keeping no life interest or other reservation for himself or anyone else. The Deed of Gift in favour of his son Wasantha Perera is to be executed at Colombo on 14 October 2022, and a valuation report dated 1 October 2022 by a chartered valuer puts the open market price of the property on that date at Rs.6,500,000/-.

added_facts.fact: The subject property is Lot 12 in Plan No. 2456 dated 3 March 1974, in extent fifteen decimal five perches, with the two storeyed dwelling house bearing Assessment No. 47/3, Pathiragoda Road, Maharagama, and Rohan Perera is its sole owner, the land being free of any mortgage or lease.
added_facts.reason: The question names no land at all. A definite lot, extent and assessment number make the subject of the deed identifiable without changing any element of the charge or the valuation.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None on the outcome. A different lot number, extent or assessment number would not alter either the charge or the statutory value.

added_facts.fact: The property is situated at Maharagama in the District of Colombo, in the Western Province, and the Deed of Gift is to be executed at Colombo.
added_facts.reason: Stamp duty on the transfer of immovable property is levied province by province. Without a province the applicable charging statute is indeterminate; placing the land in the Western Province makes the governing enactment one that is present in the corpus.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the land lay in another province, the corresponding provincial statute would govern and the provincial provisions relied on here would not apply to it.

added_facts.fact: Rohan Perera acquired the property by Deed of Transfer No. 1187 dated 12 December 1977, bought outright and at arm's length from an unrelated seller, and the Rs.250,000/- he paid was the open market price of the land and house on that date.
added_facts.reason: The first limb of the statutory value is the open market price at the date of acquisition, not the price paid. Recording that the December 1977 purchase was at arm's length lets the Rs.250,000/- stand as the open market price on that date and makes the first limb computable.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the purchase had been at an undervalue between related parties, the open market price at acquisition would have to be assessed separately and the first limb would exceed Rs.250,000/- plus improvements.

added_facts.fact: The improvements costing Rs.800,000/- were an additional upper floor, a garage and a boundary wall, all built between 1996 and 1999, that is after the December 1977 purchase and before the proposed deed.
added_facts.reason: The first limb only admits improvements made after the donor acquired the property and before the date of the gift instrument. The original text does not date the improvements, so without this the Rs.800,000/- could not be added.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Had the improvements been made before Rohan Perera acquired the property, or after the date of the deed, the Rs.800,000/- could not be added to the first limb and that limb would be Rs.250,000/-.

added_facts.fact: The Deed of Gift in favour of Wasantha Perera is to be executed on 14 October 2022, and a valuation report dated 1 October 2022 puts the open market price of the property on that date at Rs.6,500,000/-.
added_facts.reason: The second limb is the open market price at the date of the gift instrument. Fixing the date of execution and tying the Rs.6,500,000/- to a valuation as at that date makes the second limb determinate and fixes the law to be applied.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the present valuation were as at some earlier date, the open market price at the date of the deed would have to be assessed afresh and the comparison between the two limbs could change.

added_facts.fact: The gift is outright: Rohan Perera reserves no life interest, no right of habitation and no other benefit for himself or for any other person, and imposes no fideicommissum.
added_facts.reason: Removes an open question about reservations. It is neutral because gifted property subject to a reservation is in any event valued as if gifted without the reservation.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None on the value. A reserved life interest would not reduce the value on which duty is calculated.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What value should be stated in the Deed of Gift by which Rohan Perera gifts his Maharagama house and land to his son Wasantha, for the purpose of stamp duty, given that he bought the property in December 1977 for Rs.250,000/-, improved it at a cost of Rs.800,000/- and it is now worth Rs.6,500,000/-.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province (Western Province Financial Statute s.37), and Transfer is defined by s.106 of that Statute to mean a sale and to include a gift, so a Deed of Gift is chargeable although nothing is paid for it. Section 48(1) provides that where property is conveyed by an instrument, the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, so the operative figure is a statutory value and not the consideration. For gifted immovable property, value is defined in s.106. Where the donor acquired the property after 31 March 1977, paragraph (c) of that definition applies: value means the lower of (i) the price the property would have fetched in the open market on the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the date of the gift instrument, and (ii) the price it would fetch in the open market on the date of that instrument. The national Act states the same rule for gifted land in Stamp Duty Act s.71, which continues to speak to instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property because Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.13 excepts such instruments from the displacement of the 1982 Act. Section 78(2) of the Western Province Financial Statute requires the attesting notary to take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, and s.78(1) requires the facts affecting chargeability and the amount of duty to be set out in the instrument.
gold_answer_draft.application: The land is at Maharagama in the Western Province and the instrument is a Deed of Gift, so s.37 read with the definition of Transfer in s.106 brings it into charge; no exemption in s.39 covers a gift from a father to his son. Duty is therefore calculated under s.48(1) on the value of the property conveyed. Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977, which is after 31 March 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of value applies and paragraph (b), which is pegged to a 31 March 1977 open market price, does not. The first limb is the open market price on the date he acquired the property, which on the facts given is the Rs.250,000/- he paid at arm's length in December 1977, increased by the Rs.800,000/- spent on the upper floor, garage and boundary wall, all of which were built after he acquired the property and before the proposed deed. That limb comes to Rs.1,050,000/-. The second limb is the open market price on the date of the instrument, which the valuation as at October 2022 puts at Rs.6,500,000/-. Paragraph (c) directs that whichever price is the lower is the value, and Rs.1,050,000/- is the lower of the two.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The value to be mentioned in the Deed of Gift for stamp duty purposes is Rs.1,050,000/-, being the Rs.250,000/- open market price at which Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977 together with the Rs.800,000/- cost of improvements made before the gift, that sum being lower than the present open market value of Rs.6,500,000/-. The attesting notary should satisfy himself that this figure represents the statutory value and set it out in the deed, and the figure remains open to the Assessor's own opinion of the open market prices at the two relevant dates.

answer_claims.claim_text: A Deed of Gift of immovable property situated in the Western Province is an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property and is chargeable with stamp duty.
Transfer is defined to mean a sale and to include a gift, so the absence of consideration does not take a Deed of Gift out of the charge.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on any consideration recited.

For immovable property that is gifted and was acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977, value means the lower of (i) the open market price on the date of acquisition increased by the cost of improvements made after acquisition and before the date of the gift instrument, and (ii) the open market price on the date of that instrument.

The valuation rules of the Stamp Duty Act of 1982 continue to speak to instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property, because those instruments are excepted from the displacement of that Act by the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act.
No exemption covers a gift of land between a father and his son, so the deed is not exempt.
The property is at Maharagama in the Western Province, so the provincial charging and valuation provisions apply to the proposed deed.
Rohan Perera acquired the property in December 1977, which is after 31 March 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of value governs and paragraph (b) does not.
The first limb is Rs.250,000/- as the open market price at acquisition plus Rs.800,000/- for improvements made after acquisition and before the deed, that is Rs.1,050,000/-.
The second limb is Rs.6,500,000/-, the open market price of the property at the date of the deed.
Rs.1,050,000/- is the lower of the two limbs and is therefore the statutory value of the property gifted.

The value to be mentioned in the Deed of Gift for stamp duty purposes is Rs.1,050,000/-, and the attesting notary must take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that this figure represents the value of the property conveyed and must set out in the deed the facts affecting chargeability and the amount of duty.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The quantum of stamp duty on a deed of gift of land is a purely statutory question: the charging section imposes duty at the prescribed rate and the rate itself is fixed by subordinate legislation made under that Statute. No judicial authority or common law doctrine is needed. The difficulty is not the kind of authority required but that the rate instrument is absent from the corpus.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What amount of stamp duty is payable on the Deed of Gift by which Rohan Perera gifts his Maharagama house and land to his son Wasantha, and on what base and by whom it is payable.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Western Province Financial Statute s.37 charges stamp duty at the prescribed rate on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Province, and permits different rates for different classes of instruments; Transfer is defined in s.106 to include a gift. Section 48(1) directs that the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, and s.106 defines value for gifted immovable property acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977 as the lower of the open market price at acquisition increased by the cost of improvements made before the gift, and the open market price at the date of the instrument. Section 51(a) makes the duty payable by the grantee unless the parties agree otherwise, and s.40(1) requires it to be paid before or at the time of execution. The rate itself is not fixed by the Statute; it is prescribed by subordinate legislation made under it, and that instrument is not in this corpus.
gold_answer_draft.application: The deed is chargeable and the base on which the rate operates is the statutory value of the property gifted, which on these facts is Rs.1,050,000/-, being the Rs.250,000/- open market price at the December 1977 acquisition together with the Rs.800,000/- of improvements made before the deed, that sum being lower than the Rs.6,500,000/- open market price at the date of the deed. Unless the deed provides otherwise the duty falls on the donee as grantee, and it must be paid before or at the time of execution. The final figure is the prescribed rate or rates applied to Rs.1,050,000/-, but the corpus contains no rate Order or regulation made under s.37, and the Statute itself states no percentage or slab. The amount cannot be computed from the sources available here without supplying a rate from outside the corpus.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province at the prescribed rate, and different rates may be prescribed for different classes of instruments.
A gift is within the definition of Transfer, so the Deed of Gift is chargeable.

The rate is applied to the value of the property conveyed, which for gifted land acquired after 31 March 1977 is the lower of the acquisition price increased by later improvements and the open market price at the date of the instrument.
Unless the parties agree otherwise the duty on an instrument of transfer is payable by the grantee, and it must be paid before or at the time of execution.
On these facts the base on which the rate operates is Rs.1,050,000/-, and the donee Wasantha bears the duty unless the deed provides otherwise.
The rate is left to be prescribed by subordinate legislation and is not stated anywhere in the corpus, so the amount of duty cannot be computed from the available sources.
